blocks.text: A lifeguard sees a swimmer go under. Within seconds her heart is pounding, her pupils widen, her mouth turns dry, her skin goes pale and sweaty, and her stomach stops its work. None of this was decided consciously: a single division of the nervous system was switched on across the whole body.

blocks.markdown: The **autonomic nervous system (ANS)** controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands through a two-neurone chain. A **preganglionic neurone** with its cell body in the CNS synapses in an autonomic **ganglion** on a **postganglionic neurone**, which innervates the target. The two main divisions, **sympathetic** and **parasympathetic**, usually act in opposition, with the **enteric nervous system** as a third, semi-independent division of the gut. Broadly the sympathetic division mobilises the body for activity ('fight or flight'), the parasympathetic division supports rest, digestion and energy storage ('rest and digest').

**Anatomical outflow.** The **sympathetic** division is **thoracolumbar**: preganglionic cell bodies lie in the **intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn)** of the spinal cord from **T1 to L2** (L2 or L3 in some descriptions). Fibres leave in the ventral roots, enter the **paravertebral sympathetic chain** via white rami, and synapse there or pass through to **prevertebral ganglia** (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric). Preganglionic fibres are **short** and postganglionic fibres **long**.

The **parasympathetic** division is **craniosacral**: preganglionic fibres leave with **cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X** (the vagus supplies most thoracic and abdominal viscera) and with **sacral nerves S2-S4** (pelvic splanchnic nerves). Ganglia lie **close to or within** the target organ, so preganglionic fibres are **long** and postganglionic fibres **short**.

rows: Craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X; S2-S4)
Paravertebral chain and prevertebral ganglia (near the cord)
Close to or within the target organ
High (one preganglionic fibre contacts many postganglionic neurones): widespread effects

blocks.title: Transmitters and receptors
blocks.text: At all autonomic ganglia the preganglionic neurone releases acetylcholine (ACh) acting on nicotinic receptors. At parasympathetic target organs postganglionic neurones release ACh acting on muscarinic receptors. At most sympathetic targets postganglionic neurones release noradrenaline acting on alpha and beta adrenoceptors. Exceptions: sympathetic postganglionic fibres to sweat glands release ACh (muscarinic), and the adrenal medulla is innervated by preganglionic cholinergic fibres and releases mainly adrenaline into the blood.

blocks.title: A ganglion blocker
blocks.prompt: A drug blocks nicotinic receptors at all autonomic ganglia (a ganglion blocker, used here as a teaching example). Predict the effect on resting heart rate and on arteriolar tone.

steps.text: Both divisions require nicotinic transmission at the ganglion, so both are blocked. Net effect depends on which division normally dominates each organ.
At the heart at rest, the vagal (parasympathetic) tone dominates. Removing it raises heart rate (tachycardia).
Arterioles are controlled mainly by sympathetic noradrenergic tone, which keeps them partly constricted. Removing it causes vasodilation and a fall in blood pressure.

blocks.answer: Tachycardia (loss of vagal tone) and vasodilation with hypotension (loss of sympathetic tone). The effects reflect which division dominates each organ.

blocks.caption: Cardiac output (L/min) = heart rate (beats/min) x stroke volume (L/beat).

blocks.title: Tracing a sympathetic pathway to the heart
blocks.prompt: Describe the transmitter chain by which sympathetic activation speeds the heart.

steps.text: A preganglionic neurone in the upper thoracic lateral horn releases ACh onto nicotinic receptors in the sympathetic chain ganglion.
The postganglionic neurone, whose fibre runs to the heart, releases noradrenaline.
Noradrenaline acts on beta-1 adrenoceptors in the sinoatrial node and myocardium, increasing heart rate and contractility.

blocks.answer: Preganglionic ACh (nicotinic) to postganglionic noradrenaline (beta-1): faster rate and stronger contraction.

items: Most organs have dual innervation, but arterioles, sweat glands and the adrenal medulla are largely sympathetic only.
The vagus nerve carries most of the parasympathetic supply to thoracic and abdominal viscera; sacral outflow supplies the pelvic organs.
Autonomic tone: one division usually dominates at rest in each organ, which is why removing it has a visible effect.

blocks.title: Do not memorise 'sympathetic = noradrenaline' without exceptions
blocks.text: The exceptions are examination favourites: sweat glands (cholinergic sympathetic postganglionic) and the adrenal medulla (a modified ganglion that releases adrenaline). All preganglionic neurones are cholinergic.

points: Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1-L2) with short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibres; parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X and S2-S4) with long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibres.

Preganglionic neurones in both divisions release ACh at nicotinic receptors; parasympathetic postganglionic neurones release ACh at muscarinic receptors; sympathetic postganglionic neurones mainly release noradrenaline.
Exceptions: sympathetic cholinergic sweat glands and the adrenal medulla.
Organ effects are predicted from the physiology of each division: sympathetic mobilises, parasympathetic conserves.

questions.stem: Where are the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurones located?

options.text: Lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) of the cord from T1 to L2

questions.correctOptionText: Lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) of the cord from T1 to L2

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the thoracolumbar lateral horn contains sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies.
distractorRationale.b: S2-S4 contains parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies.
distractorRationale.c: Dorsal root ganglia contain sensory neurones.
distractorRationale.d: Chain ganglia contain postganglionic cell bodies.

questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies lie in the lateral horn of the thoracolumbar cord, T1 to L2. The sacral outflow (S2-S4) is parasympathetic.

questions.stem: Which set of cranial nerves carries parasympathetic preganglionic fibres?

distractorRationale.a: Only CN III in this set carries parasympathetic fibres.
distractorRationale.b: None of these carries a parasympathetic outflow.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: oculomotor, facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.
distractorRationale.d: None of these carries a parasympathetic outflow.

questions.explanation: The cranial parasympathetic outflow travels with CN III, VII, IX and X. The sacral outflow (S2-S4) supplies the pelvic viscera.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the length of autonomic fibres in the two divisions?

options.text: Sympathetic preganglionic fibres are long and parasympathetic postganglionic fibres are short
Sympathetic preganglionic fibres are short and postganglionic fibres long; the parasympathetic pattern is the opposite
Both divisions have long preganglionic fibres
Both divisions have short postganglionic fibres

questions.correctOptionText: Sympathetic preganglionic fibres are short and postganglionic fibres long; the parasympathetic pattern is the opposite

distractorRationale.b: Correct: sympathetic ganglia lie near the cord, parasympathetic ganglia near the organ.

questions.explanation: Sympathetic ganglia lie close to the spinal cord, so preganglionic fibres are short and postganglionic fibres long. Parasympathetic ganglia lie near or in the target organ, giving the reverse arrangement.

questions.stem: Which transmitter and receptor mediate transmission at all autonomic ganglia?

distractorRationale.a: Noradrenaline is the main postganglionic sympathetic transmitter.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: all preganglionic neurones release ACh onto ganglionic nicotinic receptors.
distractorRationale.c: Muscarinic receptors are mainly at parasympathetic targets.
distractorRationale.d: Dopamine is not the ganglionic transmitter.

questions.explanation: Both divisions use ACh at nicotinic receptors in autonomic ganglia. Differences between divisions arise at the postganglionic synapse.

questions.stem: Which receptor mediates the increase in heart rate produced by sympathetic postganglionic fibres on the sinoatrial node?

distractorRationale.d: Correct: noradrenaline acts on beta-1 receptors in the heart.

questions.explanation: Sympathetic postganglionic fibres release noradrenaline onto beta-1 adrenoceptors of the sinoatrial node and myocardium. This increases rate and contractility.

questions.stem: True or false: sympathetic postganglionic fibres to sweat glands release acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors.
questions.explanation: Sweat glands are a notable exception: they are supplied by sympathetic postganglionic fibres that are cholinergic and act on muscarinic receptors. Most other sympathetic targets receive noradrenaline.

questions.stem: Which statement about the adrenal medulla is correct?

options.text: It is innervated by sympathetic preganglionic cholinergic fibres and releases mainly adrenaline into the blood
It is innervated by parasympathetic postganglionic fibres
It is innervated by noradrenergic postganglionic fibres
It releases acetylcholine into the blood

questions.correctOptionText: It is innervated by sympathetic preganglionic cholinergic fibres and releases mainly adrenaline into the blood

distractorRationale.a: Correct: chromaffin cells act like modified postganglionic neurones.
distractorRationale.b: The adrenal medulla is not parasympathetic.
distractorRationale.c: It receives preganglionic fibres directly, not postganglionic ones.

questions.explanation: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are modified sympathetic postganglionic neurones driven directly by preganglionic ACh. They release mainly adrenaline into the circulation as a hormone.

questions.stem: Which combination of effects results from sympathetic activation?

options.text: Mydriasis, tachycardia, bronchodilation, reduced gut motility

questions.correctOptionText: Mydriasis, tachycardia, bronchodilation, reduced gut motility

distractorRationale.b: Correct: this is the pattern of fight or flight.
distractorRationale.d: Miosis and increased secretions are parasympathetic.

questions.explanation: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for activity: pupils dilate, heart rate rises, airways dilate and digestion is suppressed. The other options include parasympathetic effects.

questions.stem: A child accidentally ingests a plant containing a muscarinic receptor antagonist. Predict the effects on pupil size, heart rate, saliva, sweating and bladder emptying, and explain each in terms of autonomic transmitters.
markingGuide: Pupils dilate (loss of parasympathetic constriction at the sphincter pupillae)
Heart rate rises (loss of vagal muscarinic tone at the sinoatrial node)
Reduced sweating and hot dry skin: sweat glands are sympathetic but cholinergic and muscarinic, so they are also blocked
Urinary retention (loss of muscarinic detrusor contraction)
Nicotinic ganglionic transmission and noradrenergic signalling are unaffected
questions.explanation: Blocking muscarinic receptors removes parasympathetic effects on pupil, heart, salivary glands and bladder. Sweat glands are also affected because the sympathetic supply to them is cholinergic and muscarinic.

questions.stem: At rest a patient has heart rate 72 beats/min and stroke volume 70 mL. During sympathetic activation heart rate rises to 120 beats/min and stroke volume to 85 mL. Using CO = HR x SV, what is the cardiac output during sympathetic activation, in L/min?
questions.explanation: CO = 120 beats/min x 85 mL/beat = 10,200 mL/min = 10.2 L/min. This is roughly double the resting value of about 5.0 L/min (72 x 70 mL), showing how beta-1 stimulation of rate and contractility raises output.
